title: Agents
summary: What an agent really is (a model, some tools and a loop), how MCP lets tools plug into any agent, and how to tell when a plain workflow is the better build.
youWillLearn: That an agent is a model calling tools in a loop until it decides it is done
How to write that loop, and which limits it always needs
What MCP is, and why it matters for apps you sell
How to decide between an agent and a simple workflow

glossary.agent: A program where a model decides its own next step, calls tools, reads the results, and repeats until the task is done.
glossary.agent loop: The code that keeps calling the model, running the tools it asks for, and sending back the results, until it stops asking.
glossary.workflow: A fixed sequence of steps written in code, where the model fills in specific steps but does not choose what happens next.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: an open standard for plugging tools and data into AI apps, so one tool server works with many different agents.
glossary.MCP server: A small program that offers tools (and sometimes data) over MCP, such as "search notes" or "create issue".
glossary.side effect: A change in the outside world caused by a tool, such as sending an email, deleting a row or charging a card.

steps.title: "Plan my week from my notes"
body: Maya asks Notely: "Plan my week from my notes and my calendar." One model call cannot do it. It must look up recent notes, check the calendar, maybe search for a deadline it just spotted, then write the plan.
Worse, you cannot list those steps in advance. What to look up second depends on what it found first.

scene.caption: A task whose steps depend on what each previous step finds.

steps.title: An agent is a model in a loop
body: An agent is lesson 4's tool use, repeated. The model asks for a tool. Your code runs it and sends back the result. The model asks for another, or decides it has enough and answers.
That is the whole trick: the model chooses the next step each time, and your agent loop keeps going until the model stops asking.

callout.text: A detective with a phone. Each call's answer decides who they ring next. You cannot script the calls in advance, but you can decide whose numbers they have.

scene.caption: Ask model, run tool, send result, repeat. The model decides when to stop.

steps.title: The loop, in about a dozen lines
body: Call the model with the tools. Append its reply to the history. If stop_reason is not tool_use, you are done. Otherwise run the tools, append the results, and go again.
Note the step limit. A loop without one can run, and bill, for a very long time. SDKs also ship a tool runner that writes this loop for you.

code.caption: runTools runs each tool_use block as this user and returns matching tool_result blocks.

scene.caption: Each turn of the loop adds to the history. It stops on an answer or at the limit.

steps.title: Tools are the agent's hands
body: An agent is only as good as its tools. Give it a few clear ones, not thirty overlapping ones. Describe when to use each, and return errors it can act on: "No notes match 'logo'. Try a broader query."
Split tools that read from tools with side effects. Reading notes is harmless. Sending email or deleting events is not, and deserves a human's yes.

callout.text: Tool results go back into the context window. Return what the model needs, like titles and short excerpts, not whole tables. Big results make every later step slower and more expensive.

scene.caption: Read tools run freely. Tools that change the world wait for approval.

steps.title: MCP: one plug for every agent
body: Every agent needs tools, and every app has its own. MCP is an open standard that lets an MCP server offer tools once, so any MCP-capable app can use them.
You already use this: the Supabase or GitHub servers you add to Claude Code. Notely could ship its own, so Maya's Claude app can search her notes. That is a real feature to sell a client.

code.code:
# connect Claude Code to a remote MCP server
claude mcp add --transport http notely https://notely.app/mcp
code.caption: Same server, many clients. A real one needs sign-in (OAuth), so it acts only as that user. The URL is made up.

scene.caption: One MCP server, many AI apps that can use its tools.

steps.title: Most features do not need an agent
body: Agents are slower, cost more, and behave less predictably, because the model chooses the path. So use the simplest thing that works.

One model call: summaries, extraction. A workflow, where your code fixes the steps: fetch, then call the model, then save. An agent only when the steps truly cannot be known in advance, like debugging or open research.

callout.text: Clients often ask for "an agent" when they mean "an AI feature". Propose the simplest version that meets the goal. It is cheaper to run, easier to test, and quicker to ship.

scene.caption: From simple to complex. Start on the left; move right only when you must.

steps.title: Notely's planner: workflow first
body: Look again at "plan my week". Notely almost always needs the same two things: last week's notes and next week's calendar. So code fetches both, in parallel, and makes one model call.
It is faster, cheaper, and you can test it with fixed inputs. If users later ask follow-ups that need open-ended digging, the planner can grow into an agent. Start here.

code.caption: Your code picks the steps. The model does the part only it can do: the planning.

scene.caption: A workflow: code fetches the data, one model call writes the plan.

steps.title: Loops that never stop
body: When you do build an agent, assume it will sometimes get stuck: calling the same tool again and again, each call re-sending a growing history.

Cap the steps and the total tokens. Stop and ask before any side effect. Log every step, so you can replay what it did. And remember tool results are untrusted text: a note can try to steer the agent, which lesson 9 covers.

callout.text: When Claude Code builds an agent, ask: what is the max number of steps? Is there a token or time budget? Which tools can change data, and do they need approval? Is every tool call logged with its input and result? Could a simple workflow do the same job?

scene.caption: A stuck agent repeats itself. Limits and approvals stop it.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: An agent is a model choosing tools in a loop until it is done. Your code runs the tools, caps the steps, asks before side effects, and logs everything.
MCP lets one tool server work with many AI apps. And most features are better as one call or a fixed workflow. Reach for an agent only when the steps cannot be known in advance.

quiz.question: What makes something an agent rather than a workflow?

options.text: It uses more than one model call.
options.why: A workflow can make several calls too. The difference is who decides the steps.

options.text: The model decides the next step based on what it found, in a loop.
options.why: In a workflow your code fixes the sequence. In an agent the model picks each next tool call until it decides it is done.
MCP is a way to plug in tools. Workflows and agents can both use it, or not.

quiz.question: A salon owner, Sam, wants "an AI agent" that sends each client a reminder text the day before their booking. What do you propose?

options.text: An agent with tools to read bookings and send texts, running every hour.
options.why: The steps are fully known. An agent adds cost, latency and a way to send wrong texts, for no gain.

options.text: A model call that decides whether reminders are needed at all.
options.why: Whether to remind is a fixed business rule. Code can decide it reliably.

options.text: A scheduled job: code selects tomorrow's bookings and sends a text, maybe with a model writing a friendly message.
options.why: Fixed steps belong in code. The model, if used at all, fills in one step: the wording.

quiz.question: Claude Code built an agent loop with while (true) and a delete_note tool that runs without asking. What do you ask for first?

options.text: A step limit and budget, and a user confirmation before delete_note runs.
options.why: Loops can get stuck and keep billing, and tools with side effects need a human yes. Both limits belong in code.

options.text: A better system prompt telling it to never loop and to be careful with deletes.
options.why: Prompts help, but they are not limits. The code must enforce the cap and the approval.

options.text: A larger model, so it makes fewer mistakes.
options.why: Even the best model can loop or misread a request. Limits are needed regardless of model size.

takeaways: An agent = model + tools + a loop. The model picks the next step; your code runs it.
Every agent loop needs a step limit, a budget, approval before side effects, and a log of every step.
Give agents a few clear tools with useful errors and small results.
MCP lets one tool server plug into Claude Code, Claude apps and your own agents.
Start with one call, then a workflow. Build an agent only when the steps cannot be known in advance.
